expected_evidence: geological: elevated platinum (and associated Ir, Pt/Pd ratios) concentrations in a thin stratigraphic horizon (Younger Dryas Boundary, ~12.8 ka BP / -10850) across North American sediment cores, lake beds, ice cores (e.g. Greenland), and paleosols
geological: co-occurring proxies in the same layer — magnetic spherules, nanodiamonds (lonsdaleite), carbon spherules, a 'black mat' organic-rich layer marking abrupt ecological change

astronomical/model_prior: orbital-dynamics modeling and radiant analysis linking a Taurid-stream fragment or debris encounter to an airburst/impact event at this date (largely theoretical reconstruction rather than direct physical trace)
material/archaeological: disruption or discontinuity in Clovis-era archaeological sites (tool assemblages, occupation layers) at multiple North American localities coincident with the YDB layer
genetic: signatures of a North American megafaunal extinction pulse (population bottleneck/decline dated to ~10850) in ancient DNA of large mammals

oral_tradition/iconographic: low-probability candidate traditions or artistic motifs (e.g. sky-fire, flood narratives) tentatively linked post hoc to the event, though such links are highly speculative and hard to authenticate as contemporaneous

model-prior (unverified, from training knowledge): the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (Firestone et al. 2007; Petaev et al. 2013 Greenland Pt anomaly; Wittke et al. 2013 platinum spherules) is a real, actively debated line of research with published platinum-anomaly findings, but it remains contested — multiple independent labs (e.g. Pigati et al. 2012; Daulton et al.) failed to replicate nanodiamond/spherule claims, so the hypothesis is not scientific consensus
response.rationale: This hypothesis corresponds closely to the real (though controversial) Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis, whose onset date (~12,800 cal BP) aligns with the specified -10850 interval — I treat the applicable period as 'younger-dryas' since no period was given. The core claimed evidence type, geological platinum/iridium anomalies in a boundary layer, has relatively high detectability in this period (0.65) because such signals are preserved in stratified sediments, ice cores, and paleosols that survive over millennia and are actively sampled by paleoclimate/geochronology research. Astronomical evidence (0.7) is also plausible in the sense that orbital modeling of the Taurid complex is a modern analytic exercise not dependent on ancient preservation, so it is essentially always 'detectable' if anyone runs the models — though it is inferential/theoretical, not a direct physical trace of the ancient event itself. Material archaeological evidence (0.35) and genetic evidence (0.3) are moderately detectable, consistent with documented Clovis-era disruptions and megafaunal extinction studies, though causal attribution to a specific impact vs. climatic cooling is disputed. Textual evidence is impossible (0.0, pre-literate context) and oral_tradition/iconographic evidence is barely detectable (0.1) given ~13,000 years of transmission/degradation, so their absence should not be read as evidence against the hypothesis. Given that the strongest-detectability categories (geological, astronomical) happen to be exactly the ones most relevant to 'platinum-anomaly' corroboration, and that real published (if contested) platinum-anomaly findings from this period exist in the literature — a fact I recall from training as model-prior and flag as unverified/contested rather than established — I judge that the required evidence could plausibly have survived and been found. I raise the detectability adjustment modestly to ~0.58, above the simple average of the row scores, to reflect that the hypothesis's specific evidentiary claims (Pt anomaly, orbital mechanics) map onto the higher-detectability channels rather than the near-undetectable ones (textual, oral_tradition, iconographic, linguistic).
